title: AI | October 10, 2026
summary: Coverage was unusually narrow today: two developments met the source and significance bar. Ecosia is changing its model provider, while a new preprint examines how AI task-time horizons are estimated. Today’s collection yielded no additional on-brief development with independent cross-source support.

stories.headline: Ecosia switches from Mistral to open-weight AI models including Qwen, GLM and Kimi
stories.dek: The search company is moving its AI features to models served through German platform Melious.
tldr: Ecosia is replacing Mistral with a group of open-weight models accessed through German AI platform Melious, TechNode reports. [1]
CEO Christian Kroll said the change followed technical and quality concerns with Mistral; he described lower cost and energy use as goals. [1,2]
The reported cost reduction is the company’s claim, and the coverage gives no independent measurement of it. [1,2]

body.text: Ecosia is replacing Mistral with open-weight models including Qwen, GLM and Kimi through Melious, according to TechNode’s report based on a Politico interview. [1]

In a separate interview, Ecosia CEO Christian Kroll said the move is about using open models and European-hosted inference. TechNode reports that Kroll said the change roughly halved costs; no independent cost data is provided in either report. [1,2]

stories.whyItMatters: The change is a concrete buyer-side test of whether model choice, hosting location and operating costs can matter as much as a model vendor’s brand. The reported savings remain an attributed company claim.
stories.editorNote: Reported claims are attributed to Ecosia; cost savings have not been independently verified.

stories.headline: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot
stories.dek: A new preprint argues that estimates depend on how task difficulty is modeled.
tldr: The authors re-estimate METR-style task horizons using spline and item-response models over 228 tasks and 26 AI systems. [1]
Their fitted relationship between human task time and AI difficulty is nearly flat from 2–30 minutes and closer to linear elsewhere. [1]
They recommend reading horizon estimates alongside diagnostic plots; the work is a preprint, not a settled revision of METR’s measure. [1,2]

body.text: A preprint by Drew T. Nguyen and William Fithian recomputes task-time horizons for 26 AI systems on 228 tasks, using spline and item-response models to relax the assumption that task difficulty changes linearly with the logarithm of human completion time. [1]

The authors report that their fitted curve is nearly flat across 2–30-minute tasks and close to linear elsewhere. They argue that the same multiplicative increase in a headline horizon can represent different changes in task difficulty, and recommend interpreting estimates with diagnostic plots. [1]

METR describes its horizon as a 50%-success threshold on tasks measured by human completion time and notes that its suite is concentrated in software engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity. [2]

stories.whyItMatters: Task-horizon figures can look like a single capability scale, but their interpretation depends on task mix and statistical assumptions. The preprint makes those assumptions more visible without establishing a new consensus measure.
stories.editorNote: The statistical critique is an unreviewed preprint; METR’s own documentation is included for the definition and scope of its benchmark.
